Osbert Ashby.narrative: I have farmed the Ashby meadows since my father's time, and the land has been good to us — good enough that the town store and the Guild both come to me for grain. I sell to Aldric Marrow's store and to Mercy Abbot's Guild, and I keep on the right side of both, for a farmer with grain to sell needs no enemies in the square. The Lean Year taught me what blight can do; I gave what I could and I do not regret it, but I count my stores twice now.
values: a full barn and a fair price
the good name of the Ashby meadows
goals: bring in a harvest that leaves a surplus after the town store and the Guild are paid
see Roland settled with land of his own
keep the Ashby name clear of the Coldwell quarrels
learn to judge the market before the Guild sets its terms, so a good harvest is not sold cheap
Osbert Ashby.mood: steady, watchful of the weather and the ledger

relations.name: Edith Ashby
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps the dairy and the hens, and the house runs on her sense.

relations.name: Roland Ashby
relations.label: son
relations.note: A good ploughman. I want him to have more than I did.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: buyer
relations.note: The Reeve's store buys my grain and pays fair enough, but he holds the whole town's debts in his hand.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: buyer
relations.note: The Guild pays well and promptly. I keep her custom and my own counsel.

relations.name: Hal Tolley
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: He farms the old Coldwell fields and looks over his shoulder doing it. I would not trade places.

relations.name: Godric Rowan
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A proud man about his strip, but we lend each other a plough when it is needed.

relations.name: Osgood Baker
relations.label: customer
relations.note: He buys my grain for the town bread. A man up before dawn is a man I can deal with.

relations.name: Hedric Ashby
relations.label: brother
relations.note: My brother, and a hot one. He wants blood over a cut snare line; I want the steading left in peace.

relations.name: Hob Ferrier
relations.label: thief
relations.note: A Coldwell man selling hides at Ferncross that Hedric swears are his. I want no truck with that house.

relations.name: Linnet Abbot
relations.label: Roland's girl
relations.note: A decent lass, and sharp with the market terms. But a Guild family will want a dowry in grain I do not have.

relations.name: Ned Hale
relations.label: outlaw
relations.note: The one who does the threatening on the road. If his people come down on the meadows, it will be over my barley.

relations.name: Wren Ashby
relations.label: niece
relations.note: Hedric's girl, raised under my roof. She follows her father to the wood edge and I would rather she stayed by the hens.

memories.gist: The Lean Year came and the blight took the berries, but my grain held; I sold to the town store and watched the Coldwell folk come asking for credit.
I stood in the square when the Charter was read at market and thought: this is why I farm outside the walls and sell inside them.
Roland ploughed the whole north meadow alone the first spring after he turned sixteen, and did it straight.
The Reeve raised the gate-due and the carters cursed it at the gate, but my loads go in from my own fields and pay nothing.
Edith and I sat by the fire the night the Tolleys moved into the Coldwell farmhouse, and neither of us said what we thought.

stances.why: A farmer who sells to one buyer is at that buyer's mercy.
The Hales lost their fields and the Tolleys farm them; neither is my fight, and I have grain to bring in.
The Lean Year showed how fast a full barn can empty.
A son who ploughs like that should not wait for his father to die for a strip.

pastimes: walking the meadow boundaries at first light, checking the hedges and ditches
sitting at the inn over a mug with Godric Rowan, trading weather-talk and old harvest stories
watching the grain being threshed and weighing out the sacks himself
Osbert Ashby.calling: The land is my work and my father's before me — I would have a full barn and a fair price for it, and no shame in either.

Edith Ashby.narrative: I keep the dairy and the hens and the house, and I like it that way — the churn and the cheeses are mine, and the eggs go to the square with Cecily Carter's. I was glad when the Tolleys took the Coldwell fields, for someone had to work them, though I would not say so to Agnes Fenner at the inn. What I want is a quiet harvest and my son married to a girl who will not spend his inheritance on ribbons.
values: a clean dairy and a full larder
keeping on the right side of the chapel
goals: see Roland properly betrothed and set up
keep the hens laying through winter
hold the household together through whatever the town's quarrels bring
see Roland properly betrothed and set up with a girl who will not spend his inheritance on ribbons
keep the hens laying through the winter
Edith Ashby.mood: content, with an eye on the weather and the neighbours

relations.name: Osbert Ashby
relations.label: husband
relations.note: Steady as the seasons. I would not have another.

relations.name: Roland Ashby
relations.label: son
relations.note: My boy. He works too hard and thinks too little of himself.

relations.name: Linnet Abbot
relations.label: prospect
relations.note: A clever girl from a good house. If Roland is courting her, he could do worse — and so could she.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: guildmistress
relations.note: She would be a formidable mother-by-marriage, and she knows it.

relations.name: Cecily Carter
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We sell eggs side by side at the stall and share the gossip.

relations.name: Agnes Fenner
relations.label: acquaintance
relations.note: A good cook, and her sister is an outlaw. I am civil and careful.

relations.name: Sister Alys
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She sends salves for the hens' hurts and asks after the dairy.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: reeve
relations.note: He keeps half our grain money in his ledger and calls it caution. A reeve should pay what he promised.

relations.name: Hedric Ashby
relations.label: brother-in-law
relations.note: Osbert's brother hunts the wood edge for us and asks for little. I send him bread and he sends back a hare.

relations.name: Wren Ashby
relations.label: niece
relations.note: A quiet child who follows her father about the hens. She is welcome at my table any day.

memories.gist: The Lean Year: I stretched the cheese and the eggs and we ate, and I did not ask Osbert how much grain he had given away until it was over.
Roland was born in the small room off the dairy in a hard frost, and Joan Hobson came through the snow to deliver him.
I taught Linnet Abbot to set a hen's eggs once at the Guild stall, and she has a light hand for it.
The night the Coldwell households were outlawed, I heard the gate shut on them and thought of the Tolleys moving in the next week.

stances.why: The churn and the cheeses are the one thing in this house I answer for alone.
He will marry for love, but love should not cost us the farm.
The Abbot and the Fenner both buy eggs and neither needs my opinion.
I have seen one bad year and I do not want another.

pastimes: churning butter and turning cheeses in the dairy, which she will let no one else do
tending the hens and trading eggs with Cecily Carter on the square
an evening at the chapel for the sisters' calendar-days, and a word with Sister Alys after
Edith Ashby.calling: I keep the dairy and the house, and it is good work — a clean churn, a full larder, and a quiet house at night.

Roland Ashby.narrative: I plough and reap my father's meadows and I am good at it, but the meadows are his and will be his for a long while yet. I want a strip of my own — not given, earned — and I have been courting Linnet Abbot, who is cleverer than me and does not seem to mind. The town talks of nothing but the gate-due and the outlaws, and I would rather talk of a field and a roof and a girl.
goals: earn or win a strip of my own to farm
win Linnet Abbot and her mother's consent
prove I am more than my father's ploughman
earn or win a strip of land of his own to farm

relations.name: Osbert Ashby
relations.label: father
relations.note: A fair farmer and a fair father, but he holds the land close.

relations.name: Edith Ashby
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She thinks I work too hard. She is probably right.

relations.name: Linnet Abbot
relations.label: sweetheart
relations.note: She knows the market terms better than I know my own fields, and she laughs at my jokes.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: prospect's mother
relations.note: She will want to know what I bring to the marriage. I am working on the answer.

relations.name: Wulf Rowan
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We plough the same season and grumble about the same prices. He is courting Hilda Marsh.

relations.name: Stephen Hobson
relations.label: acquaintance
relations.note: He wants to build grand things. I want to grow things. We get on.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: the Reeve
relations.note: He holds back the other half of our grain money against Thornby's debt, and my father still says 'the Reeve's word.' I say a man's word is what he pays.

relations.name: Hedric Ashby
relations.label: uncle
relations.note: My father's brother, and the better hand with a snare. He keeps the wolves off our fields and never once asked for a share of the harvest for it.

memories.gist: I ploughed the north meadow alone the first spring after I turned sixteen and my father said nothing, which from him is praise.
The Lean Year, I carried grain to the town store with my father and saw the Coldwell folk in the line for credit.
Linnet Abbot showed me the gate ledger once and laughed at how the carters' names were spelled. I have not stopped thinking about her since.
I helped raise the fence round the Ashby meadow after the wolves came down the road last winter, and heard them in the woods while we worked.

stances.why: A man who ploughs another man's furrow is only half a farmer.
Her mother will hear of it anyway; better she hears it from me.
My loads come from inside the fields and pay nothing. Let the carters and the Reeve shout.
The fields do not care what the square says.

pastimes: walking out to the meadows at dusk to look at the land and think about a strip of his own
an evening at the inn with Wulf Rowan, dice and talk of anything but the gate-due
finding excuses to pass the Guild house to see Linnet Abbot
Roland Ashby.calling: I plough and reap and I am good at it — but I would rather work a field that is mine, earned and not given.
